sections.skill: Find a quantity that never changes under the allowed moves and use it to prove a target is impossible

questions.prompt: The numbers 1, 2, 3, ..., 10 are written on a board. A move erases any two numbers and writes their sum. After 9 moves one number is left. What is it?

choices.text: It depends on the moves chosen

questions.prompt: The numbers 1, 2, ..., 10 are written on a board. A move erases two numbers and writes their difference (larger minus smaller). After 9 moves one number is left. It can be 0.
Seven coins lie in a row: H H T H T T T (H = heads, T = tails). A move turns over any two coins that are next to each other. What is the smallest number of heads that can ever be showing?
Seven coins lie in a row: H H T H T T T. A move turns over any two coins that are next to each other. Give a number of heads (0 to 7) that can be showing after some moves.
questions.rule: isInteger(h) and h >= 0 and h <= 7 and isOdd(h)
questions.correct_answer: any values that satisfy: isInteger(h) and h >= 0 and h <= 7 and isOdd(h) (example: h = 5)

questions.prompt: A robot starts at the point (0, 0). Each move takes it from (x, y) to (x + 1, y + 2) or to (x + 2, y + 1). Which point can it reach?

sections.skill: Strategy: look for something that never changes
sections.relationship: Students try move after move without end. A quantity that every move leaves unchanged (an invariant) can prove at once that a target is out of reach.
sections.author_note: Students try move after move without end. A quantity that every move leaves unchanged (an invariant) can prove at once that a target is out of reach.

lesson.title: Look for something that never changes
text: Write down how one move changes simple quantities: a total, a count, odd/even, or a remainder.
If some quantity is the same after every move, it is an invariant.
Compare the invariant at the start and at the target. If they differ, the target can never be reached.

example.title: Worked example (a different puzzle)
prompt: A counter shows 14. A move adds 6 or subtracts 9. Can it ever show 20?
steps: Both moves change the count by a multiple of 3, so the remainder after dividing by 3 never changes.
14 leaves remainder 2; 20 leaves remainder 2 too, so this test does not rule it out. Indeed 14 + 6 = 20.

questions.prompt: A counter shows 12. A move adds 4 or subtracts 6. Can it ever show 15?

choices.text: No: 15 is not a multiple of 4.
No: every move keeps the number even, and 15 is odd.

questions.correct_answer: No: every move keeps the number even, and 15 is odd.

questions.prompt: Three numbers on a board are 2, 4 and 9. A move adds 2 to any one of them. The total of the three numbers always stays odd.
A move erases two numbers a and b on a board and writes a + b. The board starts with 3, 5, 6 and 8. What number is left after 3 moves?
If a quantity is the same after every allowed move, it can never change, however many moves are made.
A robot starts at (0, 0). Each move goes from (x, y) to (x + 2, y) or to (x, y + 2). Which point can it NEVER reach?

A robot starts at (0, 0). Each move goes from (x, y) to (x + 1, y + 2) or to (x + 2, y + 1). It can reach (10, 10).
Three numbers are on a board: 1, 2, 3. A move picks two of them, adds 1 to one and subtracts 1 from the other. Which quantity never changes?

choices.text: The product of the three numbers
The total of the three numbers

questions.correct_answer: The total of the three numbers

questions.prompt: Ten coins all show heads. A move turns over any four coins (they need not be next to each other). Give a number of heads from 0 to 10 that can NEVER be showing.
questions.rule: isInteger(h) and h >= 0 and h <= 10 and isOdd(h)
questions.correct_answer: any values that satisfy: isInteger(h) and h >= 0 and h <= 10 and isOdd(h) (example: h = 7)
